claims.text: A potential step from 0.4 V to 0.8 V vs. RHE can intentionally change the surface oxidation states of Rh and Ru in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Changes in Rh and Ru oxidation states alter their local electronic structure.
Electronic-structure changes shift the binding energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
Changes in adsorbate binding caused by the potential step will alter ethanol-oxidation activity.
The as-synthesized nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst is a solid solution.
The catalyst has baseline surface oxidation states before potential perturbation.
The controlled intervention is a working-electrode potential step from 0.4 V to 0.8 V vs. RHE during ethanol oxidation.
The proposed operating temperature is approximately 298 K.
Potentials of 0.4–0.8 V vs. RHE and the unspecified ethanol concentration are typical of electrochemical ethanol-oxidation studies.
Potential-induced Rh and Ru oxidation-state changes shift the d-band center.
Modified adsorption strength can facilitate or hinder key ethanol-oxidation reaction steps.
Relative to the baseline, the potential-perturbed catalyst will exhibit a distinct change in ethanol-oxidation current density.
The activity change will be accompanied by spectroscopically observable changes in Rh and Ru oxidation states.
The magnitude or direction of the activity change will correlate with the degree of oxidation-state modification and resulting adsorbate-binding shifts.
A baseline operated without the additional potential step will maintain its as-synthesized surface oxidation state during ethanol oxidation.
The proposed mechanism should hold near 298 K and within 0.4–0.8 V vs. RHE under conventional ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Conditions outside the stated temperature, concentration, and potential boundaries may introduce confounding factors.
In situ XPS can be used to monitor the proposed potential-dependent oxidation-state changes of Rh and Ru.
DRIFTS can monitor changes in adsorbate binding through shifts in characteristic vibrational modes.
Absence of a correlation between measured oxidation-state changes and ethanol-oxidation activity changes relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
